hints: Decompose the rational function using one constant numerator over each distinct linear factor.
Choose convenient values such as $x=a/2$ and $x=3a$ to determine $A$ and $B$, then verify the reconstructed numerator.
walkthrough:
Set up the partial fraction decomposition for two distinct linear factors:
$$\dfrac{5a}{(2x - a)(3a - x)} = \dfrac{A}{2x - a} + \dfrac{B}{3a - x}$$

Multiply both sides by $(2x - a)(3a - x)$ to form the polynomial identity:
$$5a = A(3a - x) + B(2x - a)$$

Determine $A$ by substituting $x = \dfrac{a}{2}$ (the value that makes $2x - a = 0$):
$$5a = A\left(3a - \dfrac{a}{2}\right) + B(0)$$
$$5a = A\left(\dfrac{5a}{2}\right)$$
Divide both sides by $a$ ($a > 0$):
$$5 = \dfrac{5}{2}A \implies A = 5 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = 2$$

Determine $B$ by substituting $x = 3a$ (the value that makes $3a - x = 0$):
$$5a = A(0) + B(2(3a) - a)$$
$$5a = B(6a - a)$$
$$5a = 5aB \implies B = \dfrac{5a}{5a} = 1$$

Write the final partial fraction expression:
$$f(x) = \dfrac{2}{2x - a} + \dfrac{1}{3a - x}$$

ai_rubric.Partial Fractions: Derives $A=2$. Derives $B=1$. Concludes with $f(x)=\dfrac2{2x-a}+\dfrac1{3a-x}$. The final result is $f(x)=\dfrac2{2x-a}+\dfrac1{3a-x}$.

hints: Integrate the partial fractions from part (a), accounting for the derivatives of both linear denominators.
An antiderivative is $\ln(2x-a)-\ln(3a-x)$; keep the minus sign caused by differentiating $3a-x$.
Evaluate this expression at $x=2a$ and $x=a$, then combine the logarithms as a single logarithm.
Use $a>0$ to simplify the logarithmic ratios and show that all factors of $a$ cancel.
walkthrough:
Substitute the partial fractions from part (a) into the definite integral:
$$\int_a^{2a} f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_a^{2a} \left(\dfrac{2}{2x - a} + \dfrac{1}{3a - x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Integrate each partial fraction with respect to $x$:
- For $\int \dfrac{2}{2x - a}\,\mathrm{d}x$: the numerator $2$ is the derivative of the denominator $(2x - a)$, giving $\ln|2x - a|$.
- For $\int \dfrac{1}{3a - x}\,\mathrm{d}x$: the derivative of $(3a - x)$ is $-1$, giving $-\ln|3a - x|$.
Thus the antiderivative is:
$$\left[\ln|2x - a| - \ln|3a - x|\right]_a^{2a} = \left[\ln\left|\dfrac{2x - a}{3a - x}\right|\right]_a^{2a}$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $x = 2a$:
$$\ln|2(2a) - a| - \ln|3a - 2a| = \ln(3a) - \ln(a) = \ln\left(\dfrac{3a}{a}\right) = \ln 3$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $x = a$:
$$\ln|2(a) - a| - \ln|3a - a| = \ln(a) - \ln(2a) = \ln\left(\dfrac{a}{2a}\right) = \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\ln 2$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\int_a^{2a} f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = [\ln 3] - [-\ln 2] = \ln 3 + \ln 2$$

Apply the logarithm product law $\ln A + \ln B = \ln(AB)$:
$$\ln 3 + \ln 2 = \ln(3 \times 2) = \ln 6$$
This completes the proof.

ai_rubric.Integration: Integrates and derives terms $\ln(2x-a)-\ln(3a-x)$; Substitutes limits in a solution containing terms of the form $b\ln(2x-a)$ and $c\ln(3a-x)$, where $bc\ne0$; Concludes with $\displaystyle\int_a^{2a}f(x)\,dx=\ln6$.
